title: Idioms, Proverbs & Phrasal Verbs
description: Master idioms, proverbs and phrasal verbs for Grade 10 boards: high-frequency expressions, their meanings and usage in sentences — with bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Common Idioms & Proverbs
topics.concept:
High-frequency idioms (with meanings):

IdiomMeaning
a piece of cakevery easy
once in a blue moonvery rarely
break the icestart a conversation
let the cat out of the bagreveal a secret
hit the nail on the headbe exactly right
under the weatherfeeling unwell
cost an arm and a legbe very expensive
burn the midnight oilstudy/work late

Proverbs teach a lesson: A stitch in time saves nine (act early), Look before you leap (think first), Practice makes perfect, Where there's a will, there's a way.

examples.problem: What does 'burn the midnight oil' mean?
examples.solution: To study or work late into the night.

examples.problem: Complete the proverb: A stitch in time saves ___.
examples.solution: nine — acting early prevents bigger problems later.

recap: An idiom's meaning is figurative, not literal
A proverb is a short saying that teaches a lesson
Learn the meaning and use it naturally in a sentence

topics.title: Essential Phrasal Verbs
topics.concept:
A phrasal verb is a verb + particle (preposition/adverb) whose meaning is often different from the verb alone. Learn the common ones with meanings:

Phrasal verbMeaning
give upstop trying / quit
look aftertake care of
look intoinvestigate
put offpostpone
call offcancel
bring upraise (a child / a topic)
carry outperform / complete
get along (with)have a good relationship
come acrossfind by chance
put up withtolerate

Some phrasal verbs are separable (turn the TV off / turn off the TV); others are not (look after the baby, not 'look the baby after').

examples.problem: Replace with a phrasal verb: They cancelled the match.

recap: A phrasal verb = verb + particle, with a shifted meaning
Learn common ones: give up, look after, put off, call off, carry out
Some are separable (turn it off); some are not (look after it)

intro.en: Idioms, proverbs and phrasal verbs are the colour of English. An idiom's meaning is not literal ('a piece of cake' = easy); a proverb is a short saying that teaches a lesson ('Look before you leap'); a phrasal verb is a verb + particle whose meaning shifts ('give up' = stop trying). Boards test these directly, and good writing uses them naturally.
intro.hi: मुहावरे (idioms), कहावतें (proverbs) और phrasal verbs अंग्रेज़ी का रंग हैं। मुहावरे का अर्थ शाब्दिक नहीं होता ('a piece of cake' = आसान); कहावत एक छोटी उक्ति है जो शिक्षा देती है ('Look before you leap'); phrasal verb एक verb + particle है जिसका अर्थ बदल जाता है ('give up' = प्रयास छोड़ना)। बोर्ड इन्हें सीधे जाँचते हैं, और अच्छा लेखन इन्हें सहजता से प्रयोग करता है।

real_life.situation:
A coach motivates the team:

Coach: Don't give up. The final will be no walk in the park, but remember — where there's a will, there's a way.
real_life.why: 'give up' (phrasal verb = quit), 'no walk in the park' (idiom = not easy), and 'where there's a will…' (proverb = determination finds a way) pack motivation into a few words. Each type works differently — and this chapter teaches all three.

TypeWhat it isExample
Idiomnon-literal phrasebreak the ice = start talking

Phrasal verbverb + particlelook after = take care of
rule_box.formula: Learn the MEANING, then use it in a sentence
rule_box.example: He turned up late (phrasal) and the meeting was a piece of cake (idiom).

reading.passage: The exam was no piece of cake, so Riya burned the midnight oil for a week. "Don't give up," her mother said, "where there's a will, there's a way." On the big day, Riya broke the ice with a confident smile. When the results came out, she had hit the nail on the head — top of the class. Her hard work had paid off.

questions.q: What does 'no piece of cake' mean here?
questions.answer: It means the exam was not easy (difficult).

questions.q: Identify the proverb and its lesson.
questions.answer: 'Where there's a will, there's a way' — determination finds a way to succeed.
It means her hard work brought a good result / was worthwhile.

speaking: The test was a piece of cake.
He visits us once in a blue moon.
The police will look into the case.
Where there's a will, there's a way.
